findings.issue: Source: "such pranks as it plays me"; candidate: "That is the kind of tricks it plays on me" is ungrammatical (kind of tricks).
findings.fix: The son of Lycaon answered, “Aeneas, I take him to be none other than the son of Tydeus. I know him by his shield, by the visor of his helmet and by his horses. He may be a god, but if he is the man I say he is, he is not making all this havoc without heaven’s help. Some god stands by his side, shrouded in a cloud of darkness, and that god turned my arrow aside when it had hit him. I have already shot at him and hit him on the right shoulder. My arrow went through the breast-piece of his cuirass, and I felt sure I had sent him hurrying to the world below. But it seems I have not killed him, so there must be a god who is angry with me. On top of that, I have neither horse nor chariot. In my father’s stables there are eleven excellent chariots, fresh from the builder and quite new, with cloths spread over them, and beside each one stands a pair of horses, champing barley and rye. My old father Lycaon urged me again and again, when I was at home and about to set out, to take chariots and horses with me so that I could lead the Trojans in battle. I would not listen to him. It would have been much better if I had. But I was thinking of the horses, which were used to eating their fill, and I was afraid they would go short of food in such a great gathering of men. So I left them at home and came on foot to Ilium, armed only with my bow and arrows. It seems these are of no use, for I have already hit two chieftains, the sons of Atreus and of Tydeus, and although I certainly drew blood, I have only made them more furious. I did wrong to take my bow down from its peg on the day I led my band of Trojans to Ilium in Hector’s service. If I ever get home again and see my native place, my wife and my great house, may someone cut my head off then and there if I do not break this bow and put it on a hot fire. Those are the tricks it plays on me.”

findings.issue: Source: "can you not be contented with beguiling silly women?"; candidate: "Is it not enough for you to go fooling silly women?" is clumsy and unidiomatic.
findings.fix: Meanwhile the son of Tydeus was chasing the Cyprian goddess with his spear in hand. He knew she was weak, not one of those goddesses who have power over men in battle, like Athena or Enyo, the waster of cities. After a long chase he caught up with her, lunged, and thrust his spear into the flesh of her delicate hand. The point ripped through the ambrosial robe that the Graces had woven for her and pierced the skin between her wrist and the palm of her hand. The immortal blood, or ichor, that runs in the veins of the blessed gods came pouring from the wound. The gods do not eat bread or drink wine, and so they have no blood like ours, and that is why they are immortal. Aphrodite screamed and dropped her son, but Phoebus Apollo caught him in his arms and hid him in a cloud of darkness, so that no Danaan could drive a spear into his chest and kill him. As he left her, Diomedes shouted, “Daughter of Zeus, leave war and battle alone. Is it not enough for you to deceive silly women? If you meddle in fighting, you will get something that makes you shudder at the very name of war.”

findings.issue: Source: "wounded me because I was bearing my dear son Aeneas"; candidate splits it into "wounded me. I was carrying...", dropping the causal link.
findings.fix: Laughter-loving Aphrodite answered, “Proud Diomedes, the son of Tydeus, wounded me because I was carrying my dear son Aeneas, whom I love best of all mankind, out of the fight. This war is no longer just between Trojans and Achaeans. The Danaans are now fighting with the immortals.”

findings.issue: Source: "Ulysses was moved to pity, and panted for the fray as he beheld them" gives no object for the pity; candidate supplies "pitied him" (Tlepolemus).
findings.fix: His comrades carried Sarpedon out of the fight. He was in great pain from the weight of the spear dragging in his wound. They were in such haste and distress as they carried him that no one thought to pull the spear out of his thigh so that he could walk upright. Meanwhile the Achaeans carried off the body of Tlepolemus. Odysseus was moved to pity and panted for the fight as he watched them. He could not decide whether to go after the son of Zeus or to slaughter the rank and file of the Lycians. It was not fated that he should kill the son of Zeus, so Athena turned him against the main body of the Lycians. He killed Coeranus, Alastor, Chromius, Alcandrus, Halius, Noemon, and Prytanis, and he would have killed more, but great Hector noticed him. Hector, dressed in his suit of mail, hurried to the front of the fight and filled the Danaans with terror. Sarpedon was glad to see him coming and begged him, “Son of Priam, do not let me lie here and fall into the hands of the Danaans. Help me. And since I am not to return home and gladden the hearts of my wife and my infant son, let me die inside the walls of your city.”
